For this one, translate everything in as many registers as your language has. For those who don't know, registers are the words chosen according to, usually, formality. It's the difference between "Sup?" and "How are you?"

Challenge: **How'v you been?"

Very formal:

¿Se'dayaude Saúje Dase aude taulaú ßau?

/sɛdajon sauʒɛ dasɛ on tolau ʃo/

How well have you been?

Which-have amount-the goodness (to)you before now?

Informal:

¿Se'dayaude'dau Saúje Dase taulaú?

/sɛdajonado sauʒɛ dasɛ tolau/

How'v you been?

Which-have(you) amount-the goodness before?

Very informal:

¿Se Saú?

/sɛ sau/

Sup?

Which amount?

And, of coarse, the answer to all of these questions:

Sau.

/so/

Pronouns generally have a 'full' form and an 'unstressed' form. It's the difference between saying "I am" as /ai æm/ and /aːm/. There are some verbs that are rare in familiar language, like the verb 'to be'. If you really want to be formal you'd pepper your speech with foreign words. When speaking with an outsider things get interesting, and you generally call people sir or ma'am or by their title.

 

Local Formal (Formal with somebody of your own region)

How are you sitting?
Ha yoe setya?
/hæː joʊ sɛtʃjə/
how 2ps.NOM sit.2pc-OBJ
Here the pronunciation of 'setya' is formal as well, the same verb would be /sɛʔya/ otherwise)

Answerː I'm sitting good.
I setmi gud.
/aːɪ sɛʔmi kʰʌdʱ/

 

Local Familiar

Are you still standing?
yat ya stenya?
/jæʔ jə ʃtɛːnjə/
still 2ps.NOM stand.2pc-OBJ

Answerː I'm still standing.
yat i stenmi.
/jæʔ aː ʃtɛːnmi/

 

Foreign Formal (when speaking with a foreigner, but you could just as well use their native language if you knew some of it)

How are you?
ha yoe our?
/hæː joʊ aʊr/

Answerː I am good.
I am gud
/aːɪ æm kʰʌdʱ/

How do questions work in your language? It seems to be verb final, with a question word at the front. Do declarative sentences keep that word order, or is it different?

In mine, you add a question prefix to the verb. The prefix, on its own, would ask "which," but you can be more specific by adding certain words to the articles on the word you're asking about. Such as in ¿Se'dayaude'dau Saúje Dase taulaú?, "se" is added to "dayaude" at the start of the sentence. Then, saú, meaning "amount" is added to "je," which is the article attatched to "Dase." "Se" and "saú," together, mean "how much," or "which amount." So, the question is asking "How much goodness did you have?" ("Dase means goodness, and taulaú means that you're talking about the past).

Questions and declarations follow the same word order. The only difference is tone. Questions would tend to have a final rise in tone, whereas declarative sentences would either not rise, or fall. "I'm still standing" and "am I still standing?" would both be yat i stenmi. It's not verb final, though. Verbs in transitive sentences with indefinite patients agree with the objects. Verbs in transitive sentences with definite patients don't agree with the direct object, but can agree with indirect objects if that's desired. Both objects would be placed after the verb if they were mentioned.
Ah, ok. So it's like "I stand," vs "I stand?".

TL;DR of the article:

  • Producers were sold the idea of a stable market to prevent volatile price swings. Thus a Maple syrup "OPEC" is formed.
  • Enforcement of this stability means some serious jackboot tactics.
  • Producers have an incentive to sell outside of the organization. Individually they can profit greatly during price peaks or bountiful harvests, but this jeopardizes the stability of the market.
  • American producers are not limited by this price fixing scheme and are threatening to uproot it.

I can understand the desire to reduce volatility and the general strategy (watching members and stockpiling surpluses) is sound. But the tactics are vile. These matters should be handled in civil court.
